column11: This quarter, SPA 2 does not include the preterit, which has been, to the best of my knowledge, posponed to SPA 3. In my opinion, preterite should be taught before imperfect because with preterite students can talk about what they have done in a specific frame of time. Instructors can ask them what they did the day before, what did they eat, who did they see, etc., instead of what they used to do, be, etc. (which is a bit more abstract).
column12: Again, this quarter in SPA 2 we have not taught preterite.
column13: As stated before, imperfect is a bit harder for students to use than preterite. Sometimes they don't get the idea that imperfect doesn't have a specific time frame, that it can be used precisely to not be specific about when something happened in the past. In my opinion, it would be easier to teach imperfect after preterite. Students might get a better idea of when to use imperfect when they have already internalized preterite and by contrast with it.

column11: This is hard to say because so far I feel like (in SPA 2), they are doing well with the Imperfect, however because we will not be continuing on with Preterite in the same class, I am not sure how this group of students will respond to now knowing about them both. Additionally, as it was designed for WQ23, Unidad 12 (which introduces the imperfect) was right at the end of the quarter. Although I had some assessment of their capabilities, understanding and mastery of the imperfect, the course ends quite soon after that making a holistic assessment of the students' understanding minimal. Right now, I feel like the students understand it fairly well, but I think the real test is to see what happens when the preterite is introduced.
column12: This is just observational conjecture, based on my assessment from grading their work, their exams, and observing them in class, but they seem to not be as confused by the imperfect at this time. One thing that sticks out is them remembering the written accent on 2nd person plural (i.e observábamos, and with irregulars like éramos). I feel like I am getting a lot of questions about accents at this time, like "how do we know when to write and not?"
column13:
It seems they have less questions, less confusions. I think the struggle comes when they are introduced to both past tenses, is when they really get into questioning "but why", "but what about this?". If I move with this group into SPA 3Y, that will be really interesting because I have been with them since SPA 1Y, now SPA 2Y, and if I get to teach them in SPA 3Y, I will be able to really observe some differences, I think.

Although right now there seem to be less questions/less confusion among the students, I think that a) regardless of which tense is taught the students will experience difficulties once the second one is introduced; b) however, I think it will be really valuable to see exam comparisons, student experience surveys, and general assessment of their capabilities with this switch, because while right now it seems "smooth" and "easy", I haven't seen this flow of grammatical tenses before, so it will be interesting to see what the results are.

column11: I believe it took more work to understand the concepts, but then they used them better. Introducing the imperfect first, made students super confused about why was not used as the past simple and that was their first interaction with the imperfect. Then, they tried to use imperfect for all the past meanings. However, when we introduced the preterit and the differenced between preterit and imperfect, the students were able to understand the uses better and how they compared.
column12: The main difference is that when we taught the preterit before, they tend to understand the meaning faster but then just use preterit for everything, and do not understand the different uses of them.
column13: It was a process to introduce the imperfect and explain that we have other forms, but overall it was overwhelming because there were many questions about meaning and use.
